name: Lactobacillus ferment

lead: Lactobacillus ferment is a bacterial-ferment ingredient used in 'probiotic' creams for calming and barrier support.
Human evidence is sparse: a scalp-microbiome study of a combined ferment is the closest found.

paras: Postbiotic ingredients are proposed to influence skin microbiome and barrier signalling, but mechanisms for this specific ferment were not shown in the sources reviewed.
No specific harms were documented in the sources reviewed. Postbiotics are not a separate regulatory category and are assessed under existing frameworks case by case [5].

brands: SWISS BLEU Relief-Calm Antimicrobial Skin Cream
label.generic: LACTOBACILLUS FERMENT LYSATE, LEONTOPODIUM ALPINUM, CALENDULA OFFICINALIS FLOWER EXTRACT, EVENING PRIMROSE FLOWER EXTRACT, CITRIC ACID

lead: Lactobacillus ferment (often listed on labels as Lactobacillus ferment or ferment lysate) is a cosmetic ingredient made by fermenting with Lactobacillus bacteria. It is used in K-beauty and 'probiotic skincare' products for barrier-support and soothing claims.

In the broader category, the ISAPP definition describes a postbiotic as a preparation of inanimate microorganisms or their components that confers a health benefit; Wikipedia describes postbiotic research as emerging and in need of confirmation in well-designed human studies [1].

Evidence for appearance outcomes is thin. The sources reviewed include a scalp-microbiome study of a combined Saccharomyces and Lactobacillus ferment and a rat study of a Lactobacillus-fermented food supplement for blood lipids, not facial-skin trials.

paras: Lactobacillus ferment lysate is listed in creams and serums aimed at irritated or barrier-impaired skin. A DailyMed-listed antimicrobial skin cream containing it with edelweiss, calendula and evening primrose extracts lists indications such as relieving redness and burning from impaired barrier function and soothing dry, cracked skin [2].

A 2023 study examined a postbiotic Saccharomyces and Lactobacillus ferment complex (SLFC) on the scalp bacterial and fungal microbiome of Chinese women with sensitive scalp syndrome, assessing microbiome changes and relief of symptoms [3]. It involved a two-organism ferment, so effects cannot be assigned to Lactobacillus alone.

A registered trial compared a postbiotic gel with placebo for gingival inflammation in people with Down syndrome [4]. No controlled human trial of Lactobacillus ferment for facial wrinkles, tone or acne was found among the sources reviewed.

A 2006 rat study of a Lactobacillus ferment of wheat, barley and kefir grains as a food supplement reported smaller body-weight gain on a high-fat diet [5]; this concerns oral nutrition, not skin. A 2018 study of natural antimicrobials in a cosmetic emulsion examined preservative efficacy [6].
The reviewed sources report no specific adverse effects for topical Lactobacillus ferment. The DailyMed label lists generic precautions such as keeping out of reach of children [2].
